utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. There are no preliminaries as far as I understand, that means that the witness can be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Keserovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. And Mr. McCloskey will now continue his examination-in-chief. Half an hour, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, everyone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, General.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'd like to see if I could clarify the situation with these three colonels that received an assignment to go to Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So could we go to 65 ter 28995. It should be page 65 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This will be your testimony in the Tolimir case and I want to start down at the bottom of the page, line 21. And you were asked by me: "Anyone else present besides you, General Mladic, and General Miletic?" And we recall this is this first night that you got back. And you say: "I'm not sure whether he was there from the outset, but General Tolimir appeared there at some point. Also present there were then-Colonel Sladojevic, who had joined the VRS a few days ago ..." Do you stand by this testimony that Sladojevic was there that evening as well?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if we go to the next page, it goes on and you say on line 1: "... and then-Colonel-later-General Ljubo Obradovic." And you say: "I don't remember if anyone else was present." But do you also recall Obradovic being present that evening as well?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Then we go down. And on line 4 I asked: "Did you hear at that point that Colonel Sladojevic had a -- also had a job from Mladic on that date?" And you say: "I did hear Sladojevic and also Trkulja, both of them colonels, and another one, Stankovic. I heard Mladic say that Sladojevic, Trkulja, and Stankovic will go to the Zvornik Brigade, assess the situation, and see if they need any assistance." Do you stand by that statement?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you actually heard Mladic say this then?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I heard General Mladic say that Sladojevic, Trkulja, and Stankovic were to go there. What I'm uncertain of, though, is whether he was addressing Miletic in order for him to issue an order to them or if he spoke to them directly. But I think Sladojevic could hear it as well, given the fact that Trkulja and Stankovic were not present.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So clearly from this, Sladojevic had not yet gone on this assignment this evening when he received it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was there at that moment. I don't know if he had gone there and returned or if he was just about to go. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, if he'd just been issued the order that he will go, he could not have already gone; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One could conclude that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So what did you do the next morning, this first morning after your arrival the previous day?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The previous morning --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Says the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- I set out from Crna Rijeka in the direction of Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. We need to get the sequence correct. You say you arrived at Crna Rijeka. In the afternoon or evening you see Mladic, et cetera. And then the next morning do you set off for Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So and what day have you always testified that you arrived at Crna Rijeka for the first time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 16th in the evening, on the 16th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And is that the truth, that is when you arrived for the first time, on the 16th of July in the evening?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, then, in July.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So if you're leaving towards Bratunac in the morning, that would be the morning of the 17th; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, judging by that it could be. I have to repeat that I am not certain whether a day passed in between and whether it was the 17th or the 18th. I cannot assert that. I just know that I received my task in the evening and that I set off in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So again, like you've said before, you received your task that evening and the following morning you set off?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So if you got there on the night of the 16th, you would have had to set off on the morning of the 17th?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, we're talking about arriving. We were talking about receiving tasks and setting off. The three are -- especially the first two are not the same necessarily. But please seek to clarify with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So, Witness, you're -- are you sure that you arrived at Crna Rijeka the evening of the 16th of July?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am certain of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you just told us that after you received a task that evening, the next morning you left for Bratunac. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct that I was issued my tasks in the evening. What I don't know for certain is whether I received the orders or the task the first evening or the next evening. In any case, I set off the next morning, having received the task the previous evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: General, this is the first time in your many testimonies and your interviews that you have ever said you didn't know whether you'd received your task the first evening or the second evening. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have to object here as well. This is misrepresentation of the evidence. This witness always claims that he is not sure about the dates and we will show it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- through his previous testimonies and statements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's not have a debate here at this moment about what was in the previous testimony because the Chamber is unable to follow it apart from what is shown to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I can agree with counsel, as I brought out on direct, that this witness has not been sure about the dates that he went to Bratunac --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- but I believe it's very important that I be able to say - and I'm sure Mr. Lukic will agree with me - that this witness has never said he wasn't sure which night he got his orders, it was always the first night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic has announced that he will address the matter in cross-examination, therefore re-examination would be the perfect moment to re-visit the matter if there's any need to do that. Meanwhile, I would have one question for you, Witness, Mr. Keserovic. If you had stayed there for one day, any recollection of what you would have done during that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During that time, at some point we also drafted a report about what we found or what we established carrying out our previous task --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. "At some point in time ..." I'm asking about possibly that day you said you may not have yet received your task and not have set off. What have you done that day if you -- if you have any recollection of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, out of the 68 months of my participation in the war, I really cannot recall each and every day. I simply cannot remember what I did and whether I did anything. That's where my dilemma comes from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you have no recollection of doing something during that day which may have been in between. Please proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The morning that you left to Bratunac, tell us about where you went and what you did?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My first stopover was in Nova Kasaba. Along the road where it forks off towards the school building, I saw Major Malinic standing on the side of the road and I stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what did you say to him and what did he say to you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told him what I was supposed to do that day, and I asked him what he was doing and what the military police battalion of the protection regiment was doing at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He told me that the unit or its main part was engaged somewhere at the front lines around Sarajevo, and that the company which was undergoing training and deployed to Nova Kasaba stopped their training and that they were deployed along the road in the area of blockade from Kasaba to Konjevic Polje and that it is where the company was at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did he tell you about any prisoners on earlier days?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did. He said that at the stadium in Nova Kasaba in his assessment there were between 2.000 and 3.000 -- or I think he said 2500 captured and disarmed Muslims, actually fighters and civilians from Srebrenica who have been coming along the road between Kasaba and Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did he tell you anything about what he was doing with those prisoners?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He said that he had organised a process of registering, of making lists of those prisoners. He also said that at some point in time it was interrupted when the commander of the Main Staff, General Mladic, came along. He stopped with his vehicle near the football pitch. He assembled the prisoners and addressed them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me take you to your Tolimir testimony, 28996, page 27 in e-court. I asked you the question: "Okay, all right, and I interrupted you. You were talking about the 12th, so go ahead." Can you clarify, what date is Malinic telling you this happened, do you remember now?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Malinic told me so that day when I saw him, but he said that it had been taking place on the 12th or the 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And your answer is this: "So on that occasion, Major Malinic told me that on the night between the 12th and the 13th, and during the 13th of July, there were 2.500 or 3.000 prisoners of war, according to his estimates ... that were located at the football pitch there ..." So you stand by that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, and I think I have just confirmed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You go on to testify: "He told me that his initial assignment was to register them, which he had started doing, he started registering them, but had to stop doing that because General Mladic told him to stop." Do you stand by that testimony you gave under oath?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So you go on to say: "General Mladic was passing on that road, and he stopped and addressed the POWs himself. He allegedly told them - he told them as well - that there was no need for registering these people because they would be transferred/moved to Tuzla because that was their destination anyhow. And Major Malinic then stopped registering the POWs." So is that -- again, is that what Malinic told you, is that a true statement of what he told you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is what I remember Major Malinic telling me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where did Malinic tell you the prisoners were sent to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After a short time, buses arrived as well as trucks in the area of the football pitch in Nova Kasaba. The prisoners were put on to the vehicles and taken to Bratunac. Major Malinic provided his escort, in other words, he used the military police to escort the buses and trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And who had ordered the prisoners to go to Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall Major Malinic telling me that at all. After the commander of the Main Staff addressed the prisoners and after they were told that they were to go to Tuzla, I don't remember Major Malinic telling me who had told him they would go to Bratunac. In his words, the buses and trucks appeared there and the people were taken to Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me see if I can help refresh your recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could go to 65 ter 28985.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's your testimony in the Blagojevic case back in June of 2004, and this was while you were testifying for Colonel Blagojevic or as a Defence witness. And Mr. Karnavas is asking you about this situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's e-court page 42, I believe. It should be 10663, it should be page 42 in e-court. Thank you. And Mr. Karnavas asked you in talking about those prisoners: "Had Major Malinic told you who had issued those orders?" And we see from the previous sentence that it was about the 3.000 prisoners, as they had been taken to Bratunac. And your answer is: "Yes. The order for the prisoners to be taken from the football pitch in Kasaba to Bratunac had been issued to him personally by the commander of the Main Staff when he was passing by the football pitch, and he personally addressed those prisoners." Does that help you remember that, in fact, Malinic -- of what he in fact told you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really cannot remember this, but I do not doubt that back in 2004 I remembered things better than I do now. It is possible that Major Malinic told me that the prisoners were to be transferred, and I think he even mentioned that the commander of the Main Staff said they were to go to Bratunac. But I can't recall everything right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would offer this one page of the transcript into evidence, given that he's a little bit still fuzzy about the recollection and this is clear under oath. If you think it is helpful for the Court, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if you consider that it would be helpful for us, then we accept that at this point in time. Of course we'll look at the evidence in its entirety. Have you uploaded this one page? Not yet?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Not the one page. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- hadn't anticipated everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, another matter is, I think you have read literally the portion you wanted to bring to the attention of the witness. And if everyone agrees that what you read is in the transcript, then I think that would in itself do -- unless the Defence considers that there's any need to have more of it in evidence for reasons of context. I see Mr. Lukic is saying no. If this is what you focused on, the only thing you read, I think we can do without.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. That's a good solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right, General, and who did Malinic tell you had ordered the prisoners to the football pitch in the first place?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for gathering the prisoners on the football pitch, he said to me that that task was conveyed by Colonel Beara. Also, I'm not sure whether he personally conveyed this to him or through the duty officer. At any rate, that was the task that Colonel Beara conveyed to Malinic, or rather, the battalion of the military police at the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And roughly what time were you with Malinic in Kasaba on this date?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, maybe about 15 minutes, 20 minutes maximum.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was this at the command post of the 65th Protection Regiment Military Police?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was in the area of the command post, but not in the facility itself but it was on the road, on the road by the school, the main road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Was this the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, may I just interrupt?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What date is this, in fact, if you are able to remember, Mr. Keserovic? The date when you were with Mr. Malinic and he was telling you all this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is that day when I was in that area. Now, was it the 17th or the 18th? I cannot say. I cannot remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. Mr. McCloskey, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Could we go to P013 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I'm very sorry, the question of Judge Moloto is not properly recorded, the latter part. I think that should be clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I didn't say "still in your office." I said: "The date when you were with Mr. Malinic and he told you about all this," not "in your office." Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Could we have an intercept, should be P01361.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You may recall, I believe you have seen this intercept before, it was from 17 July at 11.15 hours. Do you recall being shown this intercept I believe by Mr. Karnavas as well as the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had an opportunity of seeing this intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as we can see it's between two unknown persons, X and Y, and they start speaking about something, it's hard to say. And then Y asks a question that says: "Has Keserovic set out already?" X says: "We came across him on our way here." Y says: "And he hasn't arrived here yet?" X says: "Well, he must have gone first over there to Momir Nikolic." And then Y says: "... let me tell you. I spoke just a while ago to General Miletic." X says: "Okay." Y says: "He told me that Keserovic also has to come here to solve these issues." And where's -- where was -- as far as you know, if this was 17 July, where would Momir Nikolic have been, to your knowledge, if you know anything about Momir Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, I don't know anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, needless to remind you there are only a couple of minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You have testified before you knew what brigade he was from, right, though you didn't know him personally?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't quite understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You recall testifying that while you did not know Momir Nikolic personally, you knew which brigade he was from?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I knew when I found out that Momir Nikolic was the security organ in the Bratunac Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And if this intercept is accurate, there is a suggestion here that you may have gone over towards Momir Nikolic before going to wherever this other location is, correct, and that would have been the Bratunac area then?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who talked and when. I see the time, but what I said, namely, that I first stopped at Kasaba and then from there went to Bratunac via Konjevic Polje, that is correct. But -- I mean, Momir Nikolic, no, I didn't know him, I didn't see him, I didn't go to see him, I went to see Blagojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And did you see Blagojevic, Colonel Blagojevic, the commander of the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw him at his command post in Bratunac, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: At about what time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I assume it was around 11.00, 11.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did he tell you where he was going?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I remember that he first said to me what the units, or rather, what was being done that day in the zone. And he said that he was getting ready because he was supposed to go to Zepa. I'm not sure that he told me exactly what time he would go and when he was supposed to go. At any rate, he was supposed to go to Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And as far as you know, did he go to Zepa that day?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably yes, or rather, I don't know for sure whether he did. But at one point in time, in the afternoon, I stopped by the command of the Bratunac Brigade once again and he wasn't there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, a couple of minutes is a couple of minutes. So if you want to put a final question to the witness, you may do so; otherwise, move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is a key witness. I'm sorry my time was not a good estimate, Your Honour. He's been not an easy witness and I apologise for my time not being proper, but I then have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Saved by my colleagues, Mr. McCloskey. We, all three of us, do agree that if these are the crucial issues, you should have put them earlier in your examination, so as not to have any risk of losing time here. How much time would you still need? I'm hesitant to ask you even.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I can tell, Mr. President. And I -- absolutely 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 20 minutes are granted, that means until the break. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I will try to warn you sooner when I'm -- when I know that I'm going over. This caught me a bit off guard as you can see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As far as time management is concerned, you can learn a lot of from some of your junior colleagues. Consult them. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I would like to emphasise that the earlier testimony was as important as the secondary testimony, in the view of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Put your next question, Mr. McCloskey, then you do not lose even more time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right, General, can we -- what else did you do in Bratunac that day?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that my task was to find Colonel Jankovic, and while I was with Blagojevic, he showed up at the command of the Bratunac Brigade as he was summoned to do. They found him, so I met up with him during that day, or rather, after that, with Jankovic, I went to the command of the Dutch Battalion in Potocari, where Jankovic was supposed to convey to the commander of the battalion that the evacuation of the battalion would go through Serbia rather than through Sarajevo. And in some way he wanted to apologise to him because of what was happening, or rather, because resources were being taken at UNPROFOR check-points and that was supposed to be returned to him. In addition to that, at one moment we stopped at the public security station in Bratunac. I don't know exactly why, but Jankovic had some commitment there. I already said that at the public security station I came across Colonel Ljubisa Borovcanin, who was there in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Remind us who he is.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ljubisa Borovcanin at that time was Chief of Staff and deputy commander of the special brigade of the Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And was he involved in this sweep operation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I learned that units of the MUP, especially members of the special brigade, were carrying out the task of searching the terrain within the area of this operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's go to a document, 65 ter 4028 -- actually, it should be 65 ter 23272. Yes, thank you. You've got that. Back to the order that we had talked about with General Mladic, here we see a written order dated 17 July. Can we see the last page of it in the English. Do we see that it's from the commander Ratko Mladic and the date 18 February on the stamp. If we look over at the B/C/S and blow that up, it should be just -- it's difficult to see, but in looking at this order itself, I'm not sure why the English was spelled out as February because clearly the date is a number and whether that's a 2 or a 7 I think we'll just leave for consideration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But in looking at this order, is this the order -- a written order of the -- regarding of the oral order that you received, the -- from General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And we can see from this order that the first part of it - could we go to the first page in English - has to do with the three colonels, Sladojevic, Trkulja, Stankovic, to go to Zvornik. And then the last part is for you and it says: "As of 17 July, the forces ..." and then it lists the various forces "... will comb the territory ..." and then it goes on and says that: "I hereby appoint Lieutenant-Colonel Keserovic ..." When did you first see this order?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I first saw this order when it was shown to me by Mr. Ruez, I think, in October 2000, when we talked in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would offer this into evidence, but I would tell you, you may recall Mr. Vanderpuye offered a similar order but more of a -- there's some handwriting on it. This is -- does not have any handwriting and it's got a stamp and we will be able to provide you further information on where they came from, as you requested yesterday, if necessary. I believe they both came from the Drina Corps collection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections? If not, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 23272 receives number P1579, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1579 is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Mr. Lukic, are you ready to start your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am, Your Honour. I just need one minute to organise myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Keserovic, you will now be cross-examined by Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic is counsel for Mr. Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, General.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We're between a rock and a hard place, aren't we? We have to hurry, but on the other hand, we should not overlap when we're speaking. So we have to be careful. We have to bear this in mind so that we give the interpreters enough time to interpret my questions and your answers. Can we start?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: First, let us take things easy. First let us talk about functioning and then we're going to move on to these dates that are rather unclear. So we will see whether anything can be resolved on that point. Regarding functioning, there were units that were attached to the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us today which units these are?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was the protective motorised regiment, then there was the regiment for communications, then there was the headquarters administration - I don't know whether there was some other unit of that sort. There was also the reconnaissance sabotage detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: They called it the 10th Sabotage Detachment, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: From a command point of view, these units that were attached to the Main Staff, who did they report to?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These units, I mean as the word itself says, they were attached to the staff and they should therefore report to the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that time it was who?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time it was General Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said that that is the way it was supposed to be, that it should be that way. Were they indeed responsible to the Chief of Staff?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for this kind of decision, that they should report to the Chief of Staff, that is the kind of solution that existed in the previous army and it was taken over up to a point. As far as I know, at a certain point in time, command over all units, according to the principle of singleness of command, was focused in the hands of the commander of the Main Staff. At that point in time, what things were like exactly I cannot say right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. We'll just briefly look at 65 ter 25999.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's your interview of the 12th of October, 2000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: While that will be brought on the screen, may I ask one question. Mr. Keserovic, you said: "As far as I know, at a certain point in time, command over all units, according to the principle of singleness of command, was focused in the hands of the commander of the Main Staff." You say "a certain point in time," can you give a more precise date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know, I don't know exactly when this took place, when these changes took place. I know -- well, that's why these units are called headquarters support units, that they are linked to the Chief of Staff. And that is my knowledge at least, that the commander of the Main Staff after a while - I don't know how much time and I don't know when that happened - commanded all units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Can you give a rough estimation, which month, which week?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I might just get clarification as a follow-up. Are we to understand that there comes a time when the commander of the Main Staff doesn't have command of some units? Is that the evidence we are supposed to accept?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. The commander of the Main Staff always had command over all units, but some units - like the headquarters support units - according to a decision of the commander of the Main Staff, or rather, according to certain rules were linked to the Chief of Staff and that was a solution that existed in the previous army and we kept it for a while. Now, which periods were involved ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I ask you one follow-up question. In July 1995 had that change already taken place? Could you ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As regards the battalion of the military police of the protection regiment, the answer is certainly yes. That is a unit that I know was under the command of General Mladic. As for the other units, I cannot state that unequivocally, although I think that the 10th Sabotage Detachment, even at that time, was linked to General Milovanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which suggests that the change had not taken place for the 10th Sabotage Detachment. Is that how I have to understand your testimony?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To the best of my knowledge and recollection, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours explored this issue, so I don't need this document on the screen anymore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, these headquarters support units, they sometimes take part in operations, don't they, they are in action; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: These headquarters support units in a vast majority of cases, how do they participate in operations, how do they go into action? Are they commanded by someone of the Main Staff or are they resubordinated to the commanders of certain operations?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tasks to these units at the proposal of the professional organs are issued by the commander of the Main Staff. A task may contain what you referred to just now, namely, that for a certain period of time in a certain area for a certain task, they would be resubordinated to the senior commander who brings together all the activities in that area, and that kind of thing did happen indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say that it did happen, let's make it clear. Headquarters support units were then being resubordinated to the commander in charge of an operation who was not from the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think it's break time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's break time. We take a break of 20 minutes. Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we continue?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Explain to us briefly, please, how is communication between security organs and the officers in the security service different and how is it set aside from the communication in terms of -- from communication in terms of command?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Security organs are members of the command. In that sense, they usually act as assistant commanders. This part relating to staff security matters and the work of the command in all situations puts them in a command relationship with the commander. There are such tasks which I have discussed here as well, in particular counter-intelligence assignments and tasks which were based on the Law on the State Security Service. Such tasks were within the remit of security organs where professional management of security organs in the subordinate units was in the hands of the security organ officer in the superior unit. There were rules in place when and where the commanders of units are informed of such activities. That is the briefest possible explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Explain to us briefly the role of the military police in a situation involving prisoners.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: POWs under the Geneva Conventions and the laws and customs of war is something that one must count on in any conflict. Their treatment was regulated by laws and rules, inter alia, of the VRS. In units at the level of regiment and brigade, a commander's decision defines the location, and that's precisely what it's called, the location where POWs will be assembled. They are gathered and brought there by the units which had taken them prisoner or that the POWs had surrendered to. Immediate security is provided by those units. If the unit in question has a separate military police unit, which is always the case with the brigades, then the military police unit takes over guard duty at the point of assembly of POWs. At the location itself, initial screening -- initial processing of POWs is performed, which in principle is done by intelligence organs, with the aim to gather information that may be important for further combat activities. After that, the POWs are -- actually, a location is decided upon to get them out of the combat zone. On occasion, these were military detention centres. At other cases, POW camps or some other locations designed for the purpose. At all such locations in principle it is the military police that provides security for the POWs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In Bratunac and in Zvornik, the prisoners were secured by the military police. In Bratunac it was the Bratunac Brigade military police, and in Zvornik, the Zvornik Brigade MPs. Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the security organ of the Main Staff of the VRS had the possibility to activate the 65th Protection Regiment?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The security organ of the Main Staff, if we are talking about the assistant commander of the Main Staff or the chief of intelligence and security sector, under the rules that were in place, he could not have -- activate the 65th Protection Motorised Regiment.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the intelligence organ could activate the 10th Sabotage Detachment?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Neither the intelligence organ or the chief of intelligence administration cannot do so without the competent commander's approval, the competent commander being the person that the unit was subordinated to. The -- both organs, the intelligence and security organs, can organise some professional tasks and issue them to the military police units and to the intelligence organs, to the reconnaissance and sabotage units, but they cannot engage them as units without the commander's previous decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Does the security organ have the possibility to activate the police battalion from the protection regiment for certain, specific tasks?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The security organ may engage people from the military police services for certain tasks; in other words, parts of the battalion or parts of the MP unit. First and foremost, the MP platoon and in terms of those specific tasks within the remit of the MP platoon, which is the seven services we have enumerated earlier, that can be done without the commander's approval.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We agreed today that the operation commander had the power to control the units resubordinated to him. Would you agree that in July 1995, in the area of Srebrenica, Bratunac, and Zvornik, the operation commander Krivaja 95 was General Krstic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Subsequently, in the years that followed, I learned that the Drina Corps command was ordered to carry out the operation Krivaja 95. When it comes to a specific person, I know that during the initial period the corps commander was General Zivanovic. According to some documents, as of the 13th of July it was General Krstic in his stead.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The 10th Sabotage Detachment took part in the operation of liberating Srebrenica, do you know that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Subsequently I learned in a conversation with some officers that the 10th Sabotage Detachment did take part in liberating Srebrenica. However, some officers told me that it was not specified in the decision for the operation, it was not on the list of the units that were to take part.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In principle -- in keeping with the principle of unity of command, would you agree that they were resubordinated to the Drina Corps in that operation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of the units should have and probably were resubordinated to the operations commander, that is to say, the Drina Corps commander. What things were like in the field is something I don't know because I was not a direct participant. In any case, it should have been the way I described.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: After the Drina Corps operation was concluded in Srebrenica, members of the 10th Sabotage Detachment left the area and went to their base in Dragosevac village. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not, and I didn't know at the time where they were or where their base was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that they were not in the original order, that they were not in the list of units to take part in Krivaja 95. Is it correct that their participation could have been regulated by way of a separate order?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. Depending on the development of the operation, certain units could be excluded or included. It is standard practice. The commander acts by providing corrections to his previous orders, depending on the development of the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will go back to the issue of POWs. POWs are taken over, guarded, and interrogated by the security organ, who is in charge of performing such tasks in the area where the POWs are located; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe I have already said that the first contact with POWs is mostly through security organs for the reasons I've specified. Then it is security organs that are included who, under the rules, should conduct security checks of the POWs. Such security checks or processing consists of a number of different activities, starting with identification, gathering information on membership to certain units, documenting such membership in order to be accorded the status of POW under the international regulations in place. They also need to verify whether by that time they had taken part in certain activities and committed offences in that regard. They also gather different sorts of information that is necessary through interviews with each and every POW. Following it, the security organ needs to draft a document on the activities undertaken.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, is it also correct that the search of POWs is standard practice?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, disarming and searching POWs is what is done first. It is done by those who come into contact with POWs first.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can we also conclude that there is nothing unlawful in having them searched?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is nothing unlawful. It is envisaged by the law and the judiciary within any defence system, the procedure is the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put a follow-up question? How do you understand the word "search"? Can you describe the procedure for us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A POW or a person surrendering or being placed in a situation where he or she can no longer offer resistance, when called upon to do so needs to lay down their weapon, needs to step away a few metres away from the weapon, so that the weapon becomes closer to the person engaging in search. The POW is then approached in a prescribed way from the side and back. The person in question needs to spread their arms and legs and frisked through clothes in an attempt to locate any other weapons, ammunition, and explosive devices, that is to say, any kind of device that could be used to turn against the people taking him prisoner. That is the search.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And what about his personal belongings and his identification documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Any identification documents are checked and they should be attached to the official note accompanying the POW en route to be it a POW camp or if the person is to be exchanged. All documentation needs to be preserved in a prescribed way to accompany the POW en route to whatever the destination is under the rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And what about the other personal belongings? I'm not talking about ammunition and weapons, but other personal belongings.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, they're not supposed to be taken away. Usually these are small objects, perhaps money, jewellery, that is not supposed to be taken away unless these are objects that can harm others or that can be used to harm oneself. But probably it does happen that that is taken away too, but it's not according to the rules and it shouldn't be taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You answered the question about the identity documents, that they should be taken and then attached to the, as you said, to the official note accompanying the prisoner of war. Do I understand that it's your position that you could take those identity documents from a prisoner of war and not -- he should not keep it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, they can be taken away while the prisoner of war is in that status. He does not keep his documents. They are safe-guarded in a convenient place by those who guard prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You referred to the rules several times. Could you indicate to me which rule prescribes that -- or at least allows for individual documentation to be taken from the prisoner of war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm not sure now which rule regulates that, but there is no doubt that that was the prevalent practice. And I had the opportunity of seeing documents that were taken away from POWs at certain POW camps and that were being safe-guarded at the camp command. What this was based on is something that I am not sure I can tell you right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I was asking because you referred several times to applicable rules, and it seems that you now shift to the experience or the -- what you observed. Another question in this respect, since you're referring -- earlier you said about -- you told us about prisoners of war and civilians kept at a certain place. Could you tell us what was the basis for keeping in detention civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The basis for keeping civilians in the status or outside the status of POWs does not exist. Civilians should not be brought into that position, to be prisoners of war. That is impermissible. However, I have said that I heard from Major Malinic that, in Nova Kasaba, there was a certain number of people who were POWs and that there were civilians among them. I just conveyed what it was that I had heard, otherwise civilians cannot be prisoners of war unless they can be linked to combat action or if they assisted in combat. But that has to be established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because you told us that Mr. Malinic said to you that 2500 captured and disarmed Muslims, actually fighters and civilians from Srebrenica. Have you ever discussed with Mr. Malinic at the time what was the basis for capturing civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. I did not discuss the legal basis, and Major Malinic at that moment probably could not have known without identification, a lot of work, who was a combatant and who was a civilian. And I assume that he probably knew that probably in that group there were some civilians as well. Now, who was a combatant and who was not a civilian, I believe that he himself could not have known. We did not discuss it at that point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you report in any way that you had a discussion about civilians being kept in detention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as I said here, when I returned to the Main Staff I conveyed that in Nova Kasaba, at the stadium, there were about 2500 persons who had been gathered there from Srebrenica and that among them there were probably civilians too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you put that in writing in one way or another?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think I wrote a report. I do not recall having written a report, but I did report orally at the operations centre when I went to the command post of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which means that the operations centre of the Main Staff was aware that civilians were captured and were detained?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the basis of this report of mine, namely, that a certain number of people of Srebrenica were there, the extent to which they understood that this included civilians too I'm not sure, and probably I did not particularly highlight civilians because I always pointed out that a certain number of people, that is to say, 2500 people from Srebrenica, were taken prisoner and kept at the stadium and then transferred to Bratunac from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, reading your testimony, you start by saying that Mr. Malinic told you actually fighters and civilians, without any addition of probable. Then you told us that you conveyed, although not in writing, that among those gathered were probably civilians. And now in the third round you tell us that you may not have emphasised that there were civilians. That is a shift, which if you would like to explain that you have an opportunity to do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I would like to say that probably, probably, I did not highlight that, that civilians had been taken prisoner; rather, when I put all of this together, when I said people had been taken prisoner from Srebrenica, combatants and civilians, it's not that I singled out civilians in particular. So that's it. Perhaps it's a bit clumsy, perhaps in the beginning I put it in a clumsy way, civilians, highlighting this in particular. But I stand by what I said, that I was told that 2500 persons from Srebrenica were in Nova Kasaba. Another thing that I would like to say and I hope that you can take that into account and help me with this, a lot of the knowledge that I accumulated over these 18 years regarding these events, it is very hard for me, you see, to distinguish between the things I knew at that point in time and the things I know today. Today I know indubitably that there were civilians among them too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, it was not -- you told us that that is what Mr. Malinic told you at the time when you met him. But I do understand that even if you did not highlight that there were civilians, that you mentioned that there were civilians and you were conveying this information to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just take a follow-up. I thought you said a little earlier today that it is not permissible to take civilians hostage -- as POWs. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, are you able to explain to us why you probably did not highlight that the civilians were present if you knew that keeping civilians as POWs is not permissible according to the law?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as I conveyed that and the way in which I conveyed that, I really cannot recall that now. And why I did not highlight it then and the form I put it in, I really have no recollection of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I interrupt you. I'm not asking you to recollect anything. I'm asking you to give an explanation today why you did not highlight the fact that civilians were being taken amongst POWs if you knew at the time that civilians were not supposed to be taken as POWs? I'm asking for an explanation now. I'm not asking you to remember anything.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Geneva Conventions from 1949 is something I studied in detail only when I worked on certain findings in 2011 in relation to POW camps of the 5th Corps of the BH Army. It was then that I found out unequivocally who can be a prisoner of war. At the time when all of this was happening, I did not have any reliable knowledge about that. Today I know that civilians cannot be prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Let me ask you another little point. At page 28, starting from lines -- line 10 right up to line 22, you explain how the initial interviews and recording of the POWs takes place. And you said that: "Such security checks or processing consists of a number of different activities, starting with identification, gathering information on membership to certain units, documenting such membership ..." And you say these activities are carried out by the security organ. Did I understand you correctly there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first contact -- or rather, the first to interrogate POWs are the intelligence organs to gain initial knowledge about the affiliation of POWs with certain units. As for their tasks and intentions, that is what they're supposed to report about to their commander so that he could take measures in relation to the intentions of those units of the adversary, and then the security organs carry out security checks and process the POWs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That was the question that I was going to follow-up, you probably anticipated me, because earlier you had told us just that, that the initial contact is by intelligence. But at paragraph [sic] 28, lines 10 to 22, I'm getting the impression that it is the security organ that does all that and nowhere were you mentioning the intelligence -- but now you have explained it. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have one additional question. Did I understand you well that you said that as a high-ranking officer, that only after the armed conflict that you learned about civilians, whether they could be taken prisoners of war, and that you did not know at the time? Is that -- because that's what I thought I heard you say. I could read it to you if you are interested in it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I'm not sure that I understood this about high rank, but I mean, I said that when I studied the subject matter that had to do with the Geneva Conventions from 1949 and the position and status of prisoners of war, prisoners of war - if this will help this explanation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I read to you what you said, and if it's not correct -- you said: "At the time when all of this was happening, I did not have any reliable knowledge about that. Today I know that civilians cannot be prisoners of war." And you said that you studied it in 2011. By the way, which of the Geneva Conventions did you focus your study on? There are four, there are two Additional Protocols. Which one had your specific attention?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I read all of these conventions that have to do with prisoners of war --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and which is the one on which you focused? Let's just limit ourselves to the first four Geneva Conventions. Which is the one you remember, after having studied it thoroughly, is specifically dealing with prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the convention, I don't know the number, it deals with the position of prisoners of war and their status. It defines a prisoner of war, who a prisoner of war can be, and what his status is and what rights are derived from the status of a prisoner of war. That's the convention that I dealt with the most. I don't know what number it bears.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't know which, whether it's I, II, III, or IV?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, is it correct that at the time Major Malinic could not under the circumstances professionally distinguish between civilians and soldiers?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at a glance. You couldn't distinguish soldiers and civilians, especially if they were all mixed together.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know that at the time a great majority of the fighters of the 20th Division of the ABiH was dressed in civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some intelligence and some information testified to that. What the situation was with the 28th Division and what parts of uniform its fighters had is something I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know that at the time in Srebrenica general mobilisation was in force pertaining to all able-bodied men?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I learned of this general mobilisation although I'm not sure if I knew about it at the time, given the fact that I wasn't in the area for long and I didn't deal specifically with Srebrenica. But later I even think that at a trial here General Tolimir showed me a document proclaiming general mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you know that the column of men which set off from Srebrenica to Tuzla comprised almost exclusively able-bodied men?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know of it first hand, but intelligence information indicated that it was mostly men, able-bodied men that set off.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll read out a part which is from 65 ter 25999, since we have discussed the topic extensively. It is actually your interview with Mr. Ruez on 12 October 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need page 79. That is the B/C/S reference. I know the ERN number of the English. [In English] It should be page 92 in English version. Two pages less, so it's page 90, 9-0. That's at -- [Interpretation] in the B/C/S it is line 18.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez asked you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In English?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What line in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm struggling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're going to leave us behind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It could be line 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 15, 14/15, yeah. It's just the end of Mr. Ruez's question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He asked you who was the person in charge of dealing with prisoners of war. In line 19 in your version and 17 in the English, you say: "I am not sure that they were placed under the command of the commander of the Bratunac Brigade, but they were taken to the area of the Bratunac Brigade. Whether they were taken over by the Bratunac Brigade or civilian police or both. From a professional point of view, the chief of security of that brigade would be responsible for prisoners within that brigade's zone, but everything is within the responsibility of the commander." So you say from the professional point of view and then you conclude with saying that everything was within the responsibility of the commander. At Mr. Blagojevic's trial, my learned friend Mr. McCloskey asked you whether in that trial you were willing to confirm this position of yours, and you accepted the assertion as true. I am asking you now whether today you still accept this assertion as true?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is what I said and it is what I know and can remember. I think I have said so several times thus far.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Then Mr. McCloskey asked you the following question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And for that we need 1D1056.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is your testimony in the Blagojevic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 36 in e-court. The bottom of the page starting with line 24 and then we'll move over to page 37, which corresponds to the transcript page 10705. And then we'll move to 10706.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'll read out in English so that you receive accurate interpretation. [In English] "Did you mean the commander of the brigade when you said that? "A. I meant the commander who is in control of the area of responsibility. Yes, one could say brigade commander in whose area of responsibility this was." [Interpretation] I wanted to ask you whether you stand by this part of your testimony in the Blagojevic case?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Next we'll address the order issued to you by General Mladic when there was much discussion about the date; however, we'll not touch upon the date just yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We need 1D1056. In e-court it's page 29. It is the transcript of Tuesday, the 10th of July [as interpreted], 2004, in the Blagojevic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You told us -- actually, did General Mladic modify his original order?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Mladic, according to General Tolimir's words, did change the original order issued to me. So he changed the task in the part pertaining to the issue of assuming command.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: On the page before us in line 21, you said, when discussing General Mladic, whenever someone explained things to him in a rational way, in a reasonable way, General Mladic would change his decision by simply saying, "All right, let's have it that way."

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the case as regards myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Just for the record, Mr. Lukic, you referred to the transcript of the 10th of July, 2004, but in fact it's 10th of June.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: June. I said -- maybe I misspoke --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Or it's a translation issue, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, and we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- I just wanted to correct the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And this can be found in lines 21 to 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As an introduction, I would like to ask you the following. Was there anything in that order that was unlawful? And I mean the first order for which you believed you could not carry out and the second order that you actually implemented.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was nothing unlawful in it. The commander has the right to make decisions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, again let's try and make sure we've got the record correct. Now at page 40, line 13, we're saying he would change his decision by simply saying, "All right. Let's have it that way." In the Blagojevic testimony, that's not what I read. It says: "All right, it doesn't have to be that way."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will try to clarify it with the witness, but I understand it the same way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Look at the Blagojevic testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What did General Tolimir tell you? How did General Mladic take your proposal conveyed to him by General Tolimir? What did he say?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that General Mladic accepted my concern with how successful I would be in implementing the task. He said that I was not relieved from going to the operations zone in order to reach Colonel Blagojevic so that he could tell me how things were developing. I was also to report on what I observed upon return.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What was your impression? Were there any hidden agendas, intentions, or did it really boil down to reporting back from the search of terrain operation looking for members of the 28th Division?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was my understanding undoubtedly that the aim of my report was to provide feedback on the results of the operation and the results of the search for fighters and people from the 28th Division, nothing beyond that. There was no implication of anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it true that before General Mladic's order, the operation of sweeping the terrain was in the hands of Colonel Blagojevic, commander of the Bratunac Brigade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it also correct that nothing changed following the order, that is to say that Colonel Blagojevic remained in charge of the operation?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just this: It was on that day that Colonel Blagojevic had control. I don't know what happened in the days following that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That operation was also legitimate, the operation of searching the terrain; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The observation of search and blocking and destroying the enemy is a legitimate military operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Let's now look into this, we have a few minutes left. When General Mladic is not in the Main Staff, is it correct that if General Mladic is absent from the Main Staff, the commanding officer is his deputy Manojlo Milovanovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could we get clarity what he means by "absent." Absent from where? The whole zone of the VRS or just the building of the Main Staff? It really without a specificity means nothing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I just posed an open question so the witness can explain us in more details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but at the same time, of course, it should be clear what the open questions are if you -- because then the next question would be what he refers to. But, Mr. McCloskey, in the re-examination, of course, you'll have full opportunity to further explore the matter. Therefore, though it might speed up to already ask for details, the witness may answer the question. The question was whether it is correct that if General Mladic is absent from the Main Staff, the commanding officer is his deputy Manojlo Milovanovic? Oh, yes, I think you have answered the question already. You said "yes." Now -- then I would ask you the following: When would you consider for such a situation to arise, General Mladic to be absent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, General Mladic is absent when he is outside the territory of Republika Srpska or if he's outside the zone of command of the Main Staff at a place when it is not possible to communicate with him and ask him to take a certain decision. That is to say, when objectively or subjectively he is prevented from reaching a decision or cannot reach a decision related to certain tasks, then this role is taken over by his deputy, or rather, the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us what you said if he's outside the zone of command of the Main Staff, what did you consider to be the zone of command of the Main Staff at that point in time, that is, mid-July 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The command post itself in Crna Rijeka, that is to say, the command post with the facilities, infrastructure, communications centre, communications of all kinds, or one of the forward command posts that were organised in a certain period of time for certain tasks, that is the zone of the command post, or rather, the area of the command post of the Main Staff. If he's absent or if he's not in that area, then he is absent, and he is absent if he's not in the territory of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that answer. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: If I may just ask one question before we take a break. Sir, you said that notwithstanding the order you received from Mr. Mladic, it was Colonel Blagojevic who remained in charge of the sweeping operation. My question to you is: What then did you do with the order that you received? Did you carry it out or didn't you carry it out? What happened to that order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Item 3 of the order that was written on that evening, I did not carry that out. The order was written, and in the meantime a correction was made by General Mladic, which was conveyed to me by General Tolimir. And I carried out this corrected, or rather, amended order of General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, but we saw this morning that finally the written, corrected order still put you in charge of the operation. I know that you said you didn't see it at that time, but what I'm saying is, after it had been corrected you were still in charge of a sweeping operation according to the written order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Miletic wrote an order immediately after it was issued by General Mladic, and he handed it over and it was coded and sent to units through different communications equipment. We can see that by looking at different stamps. We see that it had been sent. So the original order, the first order, of General Mladic was written. And in the meantime, after a few hours, a correction was made, and later on, through a new order, that was not corrected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What do you mean that was not corrected? What was not corrected?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, a new order was not made that would include this task that I got subsequently from General Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we just verify that we have no problems in translation or in transcription. You said: "Well, a new order was not made that would include this task that I got subsequently from General Mladic." I have difficulties in understanding how an order was not made, but you subsequently got from General Mladic. It's just not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mladic issued the order and he left the area of the operation centre. Acting on his order, General Miletic wrote this up, and through communications equipment he sent this to units. In the meantime, that is to say, a few hours later, a change took place regarding the task in item 3, that remained at the level of oral communication, or rather, the oral giving of a task. So that is to say that this change was not written down anywhere afterwards, so the order remained in its original form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Going back to my original question, what did you do with the order, are you saying that even though the task was changed, the fact that you were put in charge of the operation, you did not take charge of the operation, whatever that changed task was supposed to be? Is that how we are supposed to understand your testimony, that you left everything in the hands of Blagojevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. I did not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom. We take a break of 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we will resume at 25 minutes past midday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.
