utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, we talked about the Main Staff a bit, and now I'd like to ask you whether it's correct that the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska had very few people on it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it also correct that precisely because of this scarcity of personnel, the members of the Main Staff had several duties respectively?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They carried out many parallel tasks in addition to their regular duties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, for me to understand what "few" means, "few" is a very relative concept. I'd rather hear how many there were and then we'll find out whether we consider that a lot or few.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Will you tell us, General, to the best of your recollection, how many members did the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska have?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly about the Main Staff, but by way of an example, I can take the security administration, that when it was manned fully it had five persons, the chief of the administration and in all departments one person respectively. In the department for military police up until February 1995, there weren't any officers at all. And there was a typist, a technical secretary. Every department was supposed to have three, four, or five persons within it. The situation was similar in the intelligence administration where there was also a total of four to five persons. That is what I know about the sector for security and intelligence affairs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm slightly confused by your answer because sometimes you say, "when it was manned fully it had five persons," but then you do not say how many there were. So ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When the largest number were there, it wasn't that that was up to full complement. So the largest number that they had was five.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is that what they had in fact or what they were supposed to have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is what they did have. To the best of my knowledge, there were supposed to be 12 or 13 of them there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That gives at least some of the information, but as you said, you wouldn't know for the -- I don't know exactly about the Main Staff, but you saw a shortage of staff. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, is it also correct that if one person would not be present, then others would take over that person's duties?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, these tasks or duties were given to someone, someone would carry them out.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And now I'd like to move on to the chronology of the events involved. We'll try to explain where the confusion comes from and so on. Up until the 15th of July you were in the Krajina; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You said when it was that you came to Han Pijesak, Crna Rijeka, and today Judge Orie asked you whether you could say specifically about a particular day, whether you could remember what it was that you did, if there was a day in between your arrival and receiving this order. You said that you mentioned that you were working on a report. Upon returning from the Krajina --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't think that that was the evidence. Let's check that exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Give me one second. I try to find --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll find it for you in a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Also, I don't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please. Could we first ...

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Should be page 7, line 2, if I'm not mistaken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Page 7, line 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: But on page 16 -- 6, line 16, the witness mentioned that report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He mentioned a report, but that doesn't mean that the way in which you quoted him is --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's what I'm trying to clarify since I think that it's -- that the answer is not complete.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's have a look. Let me see. One second, please. I think that -- I've got it. The witness referred to: "During that time at some point he also drafted a report" --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then I said: "Let me stop you there. At some point in time. I'm asking about possibly that day."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then the witness said he didn't remember whether there was such a day, and if there was such a day, what he may have done during that day. He did not say, as you put it to him -- and you put it to him: "You said that you mentioned that you were working on a report ..." and you linked that to this intermediate day, and that is not what the evidence was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I didn't link it to intermediate day. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let me then check that exactly how you presented that. You said, Mr. Lukic --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At least it wasn't my intention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me see. "You said that you mentioned that you were working on a report," and you said that in direct link, previous sentence, about possibly that day. But let's move on. I think matters are clear. The witness mentioned working on a report and also the witness could not put that activity on --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Certain day --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- that day, if there was such a day. Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Upon return from the Krajina, did you and the team with which you went to the Krajina draft a report about the findings, about what you found in the field in the Krajina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We definitely created the report. As I have said already, I'm not sure exactly when it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I am aware of your confusion in terms of dates, but let me ask you this: Do you think you created the report before approaching the implementation of the order on briefing about the results of the sweeping of terrain after Krivaja 95 or did you create the report upon your return from that task?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I don't understand your question, Mr. Lukic. I'm sorry. You say: "Do you think you created the report before approaching the implementation of the order on briefing" --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Implementation on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: On briefing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- search of terrain. Implementation of the order --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just read what your question reads here and correct it in its form if it's incorrectly --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think it's the easiest way if I pose the question again. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You return from the Krajina and at some point you received the order that has been discussed here, that the Prosecutor asked you about from General Mladic. Do you recall whether you created the report on your findings from the Krajina before receiving the order or after?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say either way, but I think -- and it would have been customary for me to do it immediately upon my return.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well. But these are merely assumptions so let me move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I ask then to be shown some excerpts from a footage that the Prosecution tendered. We need V000-9267. With Ms. Stewart's kind assistance, we'd like to view certain parts. First we need the time at 43 minutes, 42 seconds, to 45 minutes, 36 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please try to follow the footage and listen to the audio.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "These people were simply performing miracles. I have witnessed such cases; say a man, a soldier from Ilijas was hit right here, the bullet went out here, but he lived, somewhat more anxious, his right arm a bit stiff, but without suffering any radical damage. They have a huge ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We can stop here. We don't even have to continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but has the witness been able to hear and see what we saw --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: He said it's too loud so he couldn't follow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, could we then replay it briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mladic is telling to repeat it as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. Can we then start from the beginning, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please pay attention to ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "They have a huge number of seriously wounded people taken care of. Here are the most seriously wounded with amputate limbs, many of them entirely unable to move. It is either quadriplegia or paraplegia depending on the spine damage. I am most disturbed when I see those wounded in the head or spine. "This time we pierced it through. "We pierced it a long time ago and several times. "Yes, several times so far. The problem is not the blockade. The problem is that we didn't know each other. I have to tell you that we have accomplished in this war -- our greatest achievement is not the fact that we have so far defeated Muslims and Croats. We have preserved our people. For the first time in history our people are not standing over pits waiting to be slaughtered. I think that the greatest achievement of the Serbian people in this war is the fact that the village where my mother was born does not fight against the village where my father was born, or that a part of my family from the one side does not fire at the family on the other side. From the time of Kosovo to date, we have never had such a result. These people know that, Milan too, and Nedjo Krajisnik knows it, and you probably know it. And these colleagues of mine, officers, they know perfectly well how much I have personally invested in that respect. Nothing that divided Serbian people in the past may outlive the present time or divide us now or in the future."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We have not received any transcription. We merely read out the subtitles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, there was no transcription, but subtitles were read out by the interpreters. I therefore urge the parties to see whether that accurately reflects what was said in the original, and exceptionally, we'll proceed on this very basis. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And you should indicate where you stopped the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You should indicate where you stopped the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah, we stopped the video at 45 minutes, 36 seconds. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Can the background noise be removed, please. It probably comes from the footage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There seems to be still some background noise.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It is fine now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's proceed. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, just as a reminder, this is footage from what we've called the trial video, where we -- the parties have basically agreed that the transcript is accurate and the subtitles are as accurate as we can tell. And so that's that portion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So parties agree on that. Thank you for this information.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I wasn't sure about this, but thank you to my learned friend for helping us.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, General, we saw this footage that the Prosecution received from a Canadian Serb whose camera filmed it all on the 16th at the military medical academy. Let me ask you this -- but first I want to show you some photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In e-court we need 1D1060.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, you said military medical academy. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Military medical academy, VMA, [Interpretation] military medical academy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't know if the e-court -- the picture can be rotated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So that people are standing up -- but before we do so, you asked, Mr. Lukic, for V000-9267. On your list, document list for cross-examination, I find only reference to 9265 --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's in the e-court, it starts with 5 so we cannot see the preceding numbers. That's what I inquired with my case manager as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that is -- if there is no confusion about it -- because there it is P1147.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. The trial video is made up of several of those V's, four of them, and one of them is the one that we have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. -- do we want the people who are getting married to stand or do we want to see -- some are standing and the others --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are upside down. Yes, but I need this picture first, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a marriage ceremony which took place on the 16th of July, 1995, attended by General Mladic as the best man. And this is not disputed, either by Defence or the Prosecution. His presence is not disputed at the military medical academy either. During the proofing with the Prosecution, were you told that on the 16th, General Mladic was at a certain time of day and evening in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In every trial thus far and in each of your interviews, you honestly said that you were not certain of the day and that you were not certain when you received the order and when you appeared in the area of the Bratunac Brigade. The dates being confused are the 17th and the 18th. Can you confirm that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I cannot assert anything based on memory.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You also said that you reached certain conclusions by analysing documents alone, the documents shown to you, and that you do not have a personal recollection of the dates?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we next have -- well, perhaps we need to rotate the group photograph. We don't want Judge Moloto twisting his neck.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Just behind the bride and groom you can also see General Mladic; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Behind the groom.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General Mladic is standing behind the groom and the groom is in a white suit with a tie.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we go to the next page, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I see the date on this photograph at the bottom is the 16th of February, 2012. What's the significance of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You see the date on this photograph?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 16th of February, 2012. Well, it's in line with the case number. I don't know what that is --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Probably it was uploaded on that day, since we were -- at that time we were preparing alibi notice, so we had to upload the documents with our alibi notice. And I think that's in connection with upload to the e-court. That's my assumption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have a recollection that early 2012 there was an issue about alibi.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Apart from that, if I look at the dress of the people, I would be surprised if it were February.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And there seems to be no dispute about the presence at that point in time at that place of Mr. Mladic, is there?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: On that date, the actual time is not clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But the date is what we've agreed on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You also know Mrs. Mladic, don't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Please try to find her, and she has a specific dress, polka-dot dress. Can you see Ms. Bosa between the groom and bride?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see the bride and there is someone behind her, but I only see it partially, I only see the person partially.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now we need a still from the Srebrenica video trial at 48 minutes, 58 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that she is in the same dress, whereas Mr. Mladic seems to have changed his clothes? He's now in a military uniform. But Mrs. Mladic is in the same dress and she still has the decoration, the marriage decoration on her left-hand side which is customary in our parts?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we next go back to the footage at 49.50 to 50.23 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I wasn't aware that there was any dispute about this either. Of course, Mr. Lukic, if you give all this information to the witness to ask him to draw any conclusions, that is, of course, not what we expect a witness to do. The witness can tell us what he saw, what he knows. But whether this supports or does not support the presence elsewhere or whether this refreshes the witness's testimony -- his recollection, of course that is a matter of reasoning, conclusions, and that's not -- this doesn't play any role there. You could just have said the parties agree on the presence of Mr. Mladic with or without his wife at that same day in Belgrade. We're not feeding the witness with such information that on the basis of conclusions he can tell us anything, and that should be clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, that exactly on this topic the Prosecution was feeding the witness with information so he can draw the conclusion about certain dates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think it was mainly reference to earlier testimony --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- but you objected there and I think we did not proceed with further information to be fed. But may it be clear that the relevant information for the witness might be that the parties agree that Mr. Mladic was in Belgrade on that day at any point in time, even on two points in time, one at the wedding and the other one at the military medical academy. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It's not in dispute the date. In dispute is time, so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- we claim that he left Belgrade on the 17th --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, could well be --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- and that he reached --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But this witness wasn't there, was he?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I object to announcing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- gratuitously to the Court information in front of the witness. If you're putting your case to the witness, I think that's another matter; but offering dates could be inappropriate guidance in that context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, as I said, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will move --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At the same time, there's some merit in what Mr. McCloskey said.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will just ask kindly Ms. Stewart to show us the same video from 51 minutes, 56 seconds, because at that time this gentleman was in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the 17th of July, 1995, now and General Mladic was filmed. I'm going to ask you whether you can recognise the spot where he was filmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please have the video played now. [In English] Can we start the video, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "General Ratko Mladic, General Gvero, we came here today as a delegation representing the humanitarian organisation 'Republika Srpska' from Canada. We've come here tonight ... and brought presents, but before we say what we have brought, I would like to convey to you regards from all members of the humanitarian organisation 'Republika Srpska' and the Serbs who contributed" -- Interpreter's note: We do not have the transcript. We are just reading out the subtitles.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We don't have time now, we don't have time now to analyse the faces, but do you accept that this group of people includes the persons who were at the military medical academy the evening before that, or rather, these are some Serbs who had brought some equipment from Canada for the military medical academy and some aid for Republika Srpska. First of all, can you recognise the place where this was filmed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there aren't enough details, but I think that this is at the hall, at the command post, in the villa, in front, because I see paintings on the wall. But in every office, wherever General Mladic worked, there were paintings. Although this doesn't look like it, it may be the hall in the prefabricated building. I rather think that it's in Podkop [phoen], the villa there, at the command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. It is a fact that we cannot see very much here. Now I'd like to ask for the same document to be shown to you that was shown to you by the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 04028 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put a short question, Witness. Mr. Keserovic, we saw this video of a meeting with the Canadian delegation. Were you present during that meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So in e-court 04028. [Trial Chamber and Registrar confer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And just for the record, I showed a version of this document, but not this particular one. I showed what is now P1579.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That was what Madam Registrar drew my attention to as well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This is document admitted as P1579.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And the 65 ter number was 23272.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 23272 and then admitted as P1579.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't know if it makes a difference to Mr. Lukic but he asked for the other one, 04028. I think it's the one you probably saw with the other witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There are two similar documents, but I can use either one. Somehow one of them just shrunk. Maybe this one is better visible and I can proceed with this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: General, we see, and the Prosecutor showed this to you as well, that this was received at the Milici Light Infantry Brigade on the 18th of July, 1995 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but we think that we've reversed the translations. And since the stamps are different that -- maybe if we could see the stamp on this one, if it's Milici then we've got the right one, but I'm not sure it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the stamp would be on?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm told it is the right one. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is an order that was sent electronically and received at the Milici Brigade; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Earlier on --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, can we see this again? Let us not guess.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The instruction was shown to you from -- actually, the one that was signed by General Tolimir, P1577 is the number in this case. You remember this instruction on command and control in the security and intelligence organs of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was shown to me by Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the last page in B/C/S because that's the only one where we can see the signature, but of course, if it means anything, we can have the English version displayed too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You recognised the signature here as being that of General Tolimir; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Had this document been sent electronically, on the second page would it be received as a document that was signed by commander Colonel-General Ratko Mladic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We heard an interesting explanation here why the name of the commander is always specified. That is for the enemy not to know that the commander is or is not at the command post. If you cannot answer --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not hear the end of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, perhaps it's for purposes of camouflage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, the interpreters could not hear the last part of your question I think it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Since I was -- I saw that the witness was a bit hesitant, I just wanted to give him a chance not to answer the question. I said: If you are not certain, you do not have to answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so that was the end of your question, where the witness told us what it perhaps would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We see in this document -- actually in the previous one, so we have to go back to P1979.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 1579 you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: 1579, yes. What did I say?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You said 1979 according to the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Okay. I want 1579. Maybe I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We see from this document that in the Milici Brigade the document was received on the 18th of July. Did it happen that electronic mail travelled for such a long time or could we assume that it was sent to the Milici Brigade very late on the 17th and then received only on the 18th? Because obviously it was sent electronically; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, what we can establish here is that it was written on the 17th and that it was received on the 18th. Now, this could have been late on the 17th, and then in the early hours, although we do not see the time here, although on the original of the receiving stamp we should see the hour and minute when this was received. However, it's not here, so that would be the thing that the conclusion would be based on or perhaps there was a halt for some reason, perhaps the device wasn't working, perhaps there was no electricity, perhaps the teleprinter operator was not there to deal with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we now please see the transcript of your interview from the 12th of October, 2000. This is the first statement that you gave.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 65 ter 25999. In the English version we need page 40 and in the B/C/S version page 33. English version, starting with line 7, and the B/C/S version starts from 33 in terms of the part that we need.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: From line 20, so line 20 in B/C/S, this is what you say: "On the 17th in the afternoon at the command post in the so-called hall or 'rupa' or the G-1 building, I met the commander of the Main Staff, among others. At that time he told me that I have to show up, in fact, that I have to go to the wider area of Srebrenica, Srebrenica, Bratunac, Milici, Konjevic Polje ..." Then Mr. Ruez asked you: "Who did you meet precisely that day?" And you say: "Commander of the Main Staff, General Mladic ..." And then further on you say, further down -- actually, throughout this interview as the first moment when you met General Mladic, you mentioned the 17th of July. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the way it was in the interview with Mr. Ruez.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That is how Mr. Ruez understood things too, and when he is putting questions to you he always starts with the 17th of July. We can find that in this same transcript of the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the English version page 59, line 8, and then a few lines down, and then in the B/C/S version page 51 from line 12 onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like to ask you something about the 18th of July, 1995. I know again that there is some confusion there, but I'm going to ask you about your meeting with Colonel Blagojevic. Except for the fact that you were supposed to meet up with Colonel Blagojevic, you were also told that you needed to meet with Colonel Jankovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There was discussion of another activity, that is to say, the evacuation of the wounded from the health clinic in Bratunac and the base in Potocari; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only from the health centre in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the interview transcript of the 12th October 2000, in the English, page 44, line 9; in the B/C/S version, page 37 from line 24 onwards, and then we'll have to turn to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So from line 24: "On my way out I saw a column of vehicles of the International Committee of the Red Cross. I know that we stopped and that Jankovic talked to someone I couldn't identify, but it was said that the majority of the wounded had been evacuated and that a group of about 20 had been detained and would be transferred to the POW camp in Batkovici near Bijeljina. After that, Jankovic and I separated and I went to Han Pijesak. At that time, during that day, that was the only information that I managed to collect regarding the situation in that area and what I could learn at that moment." Then Ruez asked you: "And this is the 18th ...?" Your answer: "Yes, the 18th of July, according to my records." Do you recall having so testified in providing this interview to Mr. Ruez?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had occasion a number of times and in the last few days to read the interview. And the first time I saw it after the fact, I didn't see or find something that would not reflect my words back then. So I said so, whatever is in the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You will agree that your recollection was at its freshest after the events back then?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, my recollection was most likely. Perhaps nowadays I have additional information because here at the Tribunal I was shown countless documents, which actually created this dilemma in my mind as to the date. Back then I told Mr. Ruez what I really knew best at the time without thinking twice about omitting something or saying something that would be wrong. My dilemma was created later when, in different proceedings and during testimony, I was shown different documents with different dates and some kinds of relationships that we tried to analyse factually. This is where the dilemma arose from.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think we are on time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, we are. I would have one question for you. We are talking about the 17th or the 18th and orders given and it was all military. Now, Mr. -- in the indictment of Mr. Mladic, a number of incidents are described and the Chamber has received until now some evidence which suggest that -- well, let's focus then on the 17th or the 18th, it would not have been any different, that there were a large number of people killed, sometimes many at one specific spot, hundreds sometimes - again, I'm not saying who did it, I'm only referring to evidence which suggests that there were huge numbers of persons killed. Now, all the vague language about going somewhere and observing what happens, et cetera, it is not easy for me to understand why that issue was never part of any discussion at the time. It's all about capturing persons, but that many persons - at least that was the evidence suggests - had already been captured and that in large numbers they were killed already seems to be known to no one, and that is not easy to understand if you look at the restricted, the limited geographical area and the impact of these facts, if true, would have had. Do you have any explanation for that? Or was it mentioned, although not in your presence, or did you hear about it at the time? What -- how should we understand, how could we reconcile the evidence we heard with the evidence given about what was said during meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I know is that at that time and for a few months later until the end of the war, in the VRS, at least where I was, there was no discussion of the circumstances in which the POWs were executed. It is really something that even today I cannot explain to myself or understand how and what happened and how it was all left under some veil of secrecy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There was a veil of secrecy you are telling us. Who imposed that veil of secrecy?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I perhaps didn't necessarily mean to say that there was a specific veil of secrecy, but it was all left secret in general in terms of how and what happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you were talking about executions, you didn't know about the circumstances. But is it your testimony that no one knew at that point in time in your environment that, as the evidence suggests until now, that by large numbers persons captured had been killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my surroundings, no one talked about it and I didn't know about it until -- well, to be more specific, until sometime in February 1996 when the Erdemovic and Kremenovic trials started.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But who then knew about it? It wasn't you, it wasn't those you were talking with. Nevertheless, the evidence also suggests that it was a huge -- a huge effort to bury the bodies by large numbers. And you in your position had no idea, first, that it happened; nor that the exercise was made to at least bury the bodies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I didn't know. A few days after my arrival, if you follow the chronology, I left. I think it was already on the 23rd of July and I did not return until the end of the war to the area of Han Pijesak and Crna Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But isn't it true that it was exactly in that period of time when you were there where you could have noticed what would have happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, what I saw and what I heard and to the best of my recollection, it is all what I shared with you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And about being told that there were large numbers of people gathered at a football pitch and not having any idea about what happened to them didn't ring any bell, didn't raise any question: What happened with those in Nova Kasaba I was told about? Do we have problems in finding accommodation for these prisoners of war? What should we do about it? None of these matters ever was part of any discussion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On that day or in the course of those few days, I had information that in terms of accommodating the POWs, the Batkovic camp was being set up near Bijeljina. Given the fact that the POWs were transported to Bratunac, I wasn't interested in it any further, but it was my conviction that they were then transported further to Batkovic and up north via Zvornik and Bijeljina, that is to say, a village near Bijeljina where the camp was. I simply didn't discuss it any further with anyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You never heard that many did not arrive there? Large numbers you would have to accommodate but -- what was the capacity of Batkovic camp?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the capacity, perhaps it could have -- it was an old farmer's co-operative with a few wooden huts. I don't think it could have housed more than 2.000. I don't know exactly. I don't think more could have fitted there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When was it ready? You said it was set up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The camp had existed as early as 1992 and it remained in operation until the end of the war, as far as I know. In passing by en route from the Krajina to Han Pijesak on the 16th of July, I dropped by the military police battalion and its barracks and I have in mind the MP battalion of the East Bosnia Corps. That is what I testified about previously. It is there that one of the officers from the battalion told me that a part of the unit had been sent to assist the Zvornik Brigade with their activities because they had to cover the line from Zepa, Srebrenica, and further afield and that -- those remaining were preparing themselves to secure the prisoners that were supposed to arrive to the Batkovic camp. I've testified about it earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said it was being set up. Who told you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One of the officers of the 3rd MP Battalion or the MP battalion of the East Bosnia Corps. It wasn't setting up but preparing the area and preparing the unit to receive such numbers of POWs, probably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And at the same time they were ready by, as the evidence suggests until now, they were by -- perhaps by the thousands were dead bodies to be taken care of which didn't need to be accommodated any further in any camp. Nevertheless, you say that the situation at the time, people were focused on preparing accommodation for prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is what I heard that day and what I knew. I had no other information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. I think I went a bit beyond the break time. I should have perhaps not have done that but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take the break first. The witness may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at five minutes to 2.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. [The witness takes the stand].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Keserovic, Judge Moloto has one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Keserovic, at page 70 today, lines 11 to 18, in answering a question you said, amongst other things: "Given the fact that the POWs were transported to Bratunac, I wasn't interested in it any further." And then of course we carried on. And I just wanted to make sure, were you correctly transcribed, that you said you are not interested in it any further?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think that I ended with that, I mean my knowledge concerning the POWs. I didn't deal with that anymore because when I came to Bratunac they were no longer there -- or rather, I did not know where they were and whether they were -- well, so that is where my interest in them ended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now, I have a question for you. Now, you told us this morning that the responsibility for POWs rests with the security organ. You've told us this -- we've also heard evidence that you were given an order by Mr. Mladic to look after these people, to go and sweep the area, and look after that. You have told us that you handed over this job to Blagojevic and you [Realtime transcript read in error "he"] didn't do it. Now they go to Bratunac and not to Batkovici and then you are not interested in it. My question to you is: What did you see your responsibility to be now that -- because you were in the security organ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My position was in the security administration, in the Main Staff, in the department for military police. And from that aspect, I did belong to the security service. General Mladic did not make me the person in charge of POWs and I've said that. Also, I do not remember saying that Blagojevic did not complete that task. I said that I know that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I didn't say so either. I said you left the job in his hands; that's what you told us. My attention has just been brought to -- in fact, to the evidence where you actually said Blagojevic didn't ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There seems to be a small mistake.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I will then have misspoke if I did say so. I was -- I meant to say you didn't do it, you handed it over to Blagojevic. I'm sorry. Okay. You can carry on. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So on that day, Blagojevic continued carrying out that task, as he had done during the previous days, and everything that had to do with that task was his concern, his obligation. It is from him that I was supposed to receive information as to whether the sweeping of the terrain had continued and whether the units were still under this blockade and whether he was carrying that out, or rather, implementing the task. And then that is what I was supposed to report back at the Main Staff once I got back. I was supposed to say what Blagojevic said. As for this task specifically, the POWs, I did not have that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do I understand you clearly that Blagojevic was -- reports to you? Or was supposed to report to you and you would then report to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. He was supposed to inform me, he was supposed to provide information to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sure. And for what purpose, if he was not reporting to you, because he can report directly what he has done to his superior? For what purpose was he supposed to give you any information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, they brought us into this relationship through this task. They -- the command brought us into this situation, that I should go to him and take that information from him. Why it was that day -- that way, I really cannot say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But we're hearing -- or at least I'm hearing this for the first time, that you were brought into this relationship by the command so that you must get information from him. The last I heard, you were given the task to you were supposed to go and sweep and you didn't do it; you handed it over to him. That's what you testified this morning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. I don't know whether it was reflected that way, but I did not say that. I said that the task related to the take-over of the command, sweeping the area, "pretres," not "ciscenje," and the blockade, I did not carry that out and that task in relation to me had been changed, and Blagojevic continued implementing that task because previously he had been doing it too. So it's not that I was given this task ultimately, to take-over command and to carry out a search, sweep, blockade of the 28th Division.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But this in addition to the last question. You were supposed to receive information about how it went on, so as to be able to report further up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, on the spot I was supposed to receive information from Blagojevic, and upon returning to the Main Staff I was supposed to report at the Main Staff what it was that I had seen and heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Now it's my turn just for one additional question. Sorry. You said Blagojevic was supposed to inform you about what was going on. What did he tell you? How -- what information did you receive from him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I think that I've already presented that previously, but Blagojevic said to me that that morning, the implementation of that task continued, that the units were still at the line of blockade that had been established previously, and that from the direction of Bratunac and then Srebrenica, there were forces of the Ministry of the Interior that were coming and that they were searching that terrain and that this activity was underway. As for results, there was no mention, or rather, at the moment when I was with him, he did not have any information about the results of this search on that day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Did he tell you anything about what happened with the prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember that, that he said anything about prisoners of war. I know that we were making comments, or rather, talking only about part of the population that during those days, the previous days, the 11th, 12th, were in Potocari and that were evacuated from there. I do not remember that we discussed prisoners of war specifically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: My turn now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, it's your turn, you cross-examine the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have only a couple minutes so I cannot start anything substantial. I'll try to cover some leftovers.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, is it correct that as for the operation in Srebrenica, Krivaja 95, you learned about it only from the media?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that at that time, generally, it was hard to learn about things that you were not directly involved in?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can be put that way, quite simply. What was not directly related to someone was not conveyed to him at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that at that time, although to a lesser degree, the NATO air-strikes had already started, the air-strikes against the positions of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already had that question here. I know that there were threats concerning air-strikes. Now, whether the bombing had actually started already, I'm not sure in terms of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that soon after this happened, the Krajina fell in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I witnessed those developments myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The VRS lost an entire front there; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or rather, got another front.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Got another front. After the fall of the Krajina, were you involved in these developments and the establishment of this new front line?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was at the forward command post of the Main Staff in Drvar and then, as the front line moved, all the way up until the end of the war I was in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You worked with the commission of Republika Srpska for discovering the truth about Srebrenica; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that as regards the details related to what happened in Srebrenica, you found out about that only several years after the war?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct, considerably later, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now something in relation to comments from that time, that is to say, July 1995. Is it correct that among the officers of the Army of Republika Srpska it was being said that the prisoners would be transported or transferred to the POW camp in Batkovici?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I heard too, in Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: While you worked with the commission of Republika Srpska on discovering the truth in Srebrenica, in the work of that commission did you ever come across any information to the effect that General Ratko Mladic had ordered the killing of the Muslims from Srebrenica who had been imprisoned?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I never came across any kind of document like that or any kind of order or report.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you hear something like that from anyone?

utterances.speaker: DRAGOMIR KESEROVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you for today. We'll have to continue tomorrow. It's time to call it a day for now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Keserovic, we'll adjourn for the day and we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.30. And I give you the same instructions as I did yesterday, that is, that you should not speak or communicate with whomever about your testimony, whether already given or still to be given. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, could you give us any indication about tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Less than I asked for, for sure, but I think that I can finish in one hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In one hour, so first session approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: First session. It's one hour, sometimes it's more than one session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Sometimes it's more than one session, yes. You have a very gentle way of reminding me on my time management now and then and I accept that. We adjourn for the day and we'll resume tomorrow, Wednesday, the 19th of June, at 9.30 in the morning in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 19th day of June, 2013, at 9.30 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.16 p.m.,
